findings.evidence: "The branch managers' working group audits renewal rates on the first of every month... Branch-level totals roll up into the consortium's shared reporting dashboard."
findings.fix: Either cut this section or replace it with the actual renewal-rate/checkout-volume figures it alludes to and connect them explicitly to the fines argument.
findings.location: "Circulation Trends" section (paragraphs 1 - 2, before "What the Pilot Showed")
findings.violation: This section states that monitoring processes exist but presents no actual figures or findings, and nothing here is referenced again or used to support the recommendation - it's disconnected filler.

findings.evidence: "compared with 87 percent at the branches that kept fines in place over the same period"
findings.fix: State explicitly which and how many branches make up the comparison group and note any relevant differences from the pilot branches.
findings.violation: The comparison group is never defined - it's unclear how many branches this is, whether they are the other five consortium branches, and whether they are comparable to the pilot branches in size, demographics, or item mix.

findings.evidence: "before the pilot to 5 percent after it... The survey was administered at the same pilot branches immediately before and twelve months into the pilot."
findings.fix: Either report a 16-month (end-of-pilot) survey result or explicitly flag the 4-month gap and explain why it doesn't undermine the comparison.
findings.violation: The pilot ran 16 months but the "after" survey was taken at month 12, so the avoidance-rate figure doesn't cover the same period as the 94%/87% return-rate comparison, weakening the claim that the two results are a matched "parallel" measure.

findings.evidence: "self-reported avoidance... dropped from 22 percent of respondents before the pilot to 5 percent after it"
findings.fix: Report the number of respondents (and response rate) for each survey wave.
findings.violation: No sample size or response rate is given for the survey, so the precision and reliability of the 22%→5% change can't be assessed.

findings.evidence: "replacing the current fine notices with automatic email reminders sent three, seven, and fourteen days after the due date"
findings.fix: Specify a fallback channel (mail, text, phone) for patrons without email on file.
findings.violation: The plan assumes all patrons have a usable email on file and gives no fallback for patrons without one, which could leave some patrons with no notice at all once fine notices are removed.

findings.evidence: "applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date... matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established"
findings.fix: Either cite the specific pilot data (e.g., a return-time distribution) that justifies the 60-day threshold, or drop the claim that it matches the pilot's established pattern.
findings.violation: No 60-day window, or any specific time threshold, appears anywhere in the "What the Pilot Showed" section, so the claim that this cutoff "matches" the pilot data is unsupported by the evidence presented.

findings.evidence: "Removing the financial penalty for late returns predictably increases both on-time return rates and overall program participation, which is the reason the pilot's... results... support ending fines for the whole consortium"
findings.fix: Separate the empirical pilot finding from the generalization argument, and justify the generalization with independent evidence (e.g., branch similarity, the cited external brief's actual findings) rather than restating the conclusion as its own premise.
findings.location: "Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide," first paragraph
findings.violation: This is circular reasoning - it asserts the general causal claim (that removing fines increases return rates) as the justification for generalizing the very pilot result that was supposed to be evidence for that claim.

findings.evidence: "documented in the Tri-County Library Data Cooperative's 2023 fines-elimination research brief, which reviewed return-rate data from fourteen library systems"
findings.fix: Summarize the brief's specific quantitative findings and explain how they align with the pilot's results.
findings.location: "Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide," second paragraph
findings.violation: The brief is cited as support but none of its actual findings (effect sizes, direction, consistency across the fourteen systems) are reported, so the citation functions as an appeal to authority rather than evidence.

findings.evidence: "the stronger choice is a systemwide end to overdue fines across all ten consortium branches" (Recommendation) relying on a pilot at only 5 of the 10 branches
findings.fix: Explain the pilot branch selection process and compare pilot branches to non-pilot branches on relevant characteristics (size, patron demographics, collection type) to support generalization.
findings.location: "Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide" (section as a whole)
findings.violation: The document never addresses how the 5 pilot branches were selected or whether they're representative of the other 5 branches, leaving open the possibility of selection bias in generalizing the result systemwide.

findings.evidence: "the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending"
findings.fix: Correct the branch count to match the figure given in "What the Pilot Showed" (or explain why only four of the five pilot branches are included in this analysis).
findings.violation: This contradicts the earlier statement that the pilot covered "5 branches," creating an unresolved numerical inconsistency.
